concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: A single image contains a lot of information that, in most cases, is enough to estimate metric 3D information from a single 2D image.
concepts.content:
In this chapter we have shown how to use geometric image features such as vanishing points and the horizon line, along with projective invariants like the cross-ratio, to estimate 3D scene properties from a single image. However, most of these steps required some manual intervention. All of these steps can be performed fully automatically by training detectors to localize the full extent of an object, as will be discussed in the section on object recognition, and by detecting points of contact between objects.

One of the key insights from this chapter is that a single image contains a lot of information that, in most cases, is enough to estimate metric 3D information from a single 2D image. In the next chapter, we will discuss learning-based methods for 3D estimation from images.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how to extract 3D scene properties from a single image is crucial for advancing computer vision and automating 3D reconstruction processes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Geometric features and projective invariants help estimate 3D properties from one image.
- Manual steps can be automated using trained detectors.
- Single images often contain sufficient information for metric 3D estimation.

concepts.title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
concepts.one_liner: We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane.
concepts.content:
Where should we position the tick marks that correspond to 1, 2, 3, ... meters from the origin on each axis in @fig-office_world_calibration? Simply placing them at evenly spaced intervals along the axis in the image won't be correct. Due to geometric distortion introduced by perspective projection, the tick marks are not evenly spaced within the image plane. This distortion affects each axis in a distinct manner.

Let's start assuming we know the location of some arbitrary 3D distance to the origin on each axis that we will denote by $\alpha_X$, $\alpha_Y$ and $\alpha_Z$. The question is, where do we place the ticks for $k\alpha_X$, $k\alpha_Y$ and $k\alpha_Z$ for all $k$? We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane. For doing this we will need the location of the horizon line of a reference plane (i.e. the ground plane), the position of the orthogonal vanishing point and the real measure of one object in the scene.

As shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (a) we can use the cross-ratio to estimate the location of the points $Y= k \alpha_X$ where $\alpha_X$ is an arbitrary constant as shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (b), and the corresponding image location $r$, for $k=1$, is chosen arbitrarily as shown in @fig-axis_calibration_procedure (a). Due to perspective projection, the image projection of the point $Y= k \alpha_X$ will not be evenly spaced in the image. In this particular example we chose the orientation of the world axis in image coordinates to be aligned with the location of the vanishing points.

(see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.)

In order to calibrate the axis we need to know the dimensions of an object in the scene. We need measurements along the three axis. In this example, we used the bookshelf height (197 cm) and the radius of the table base (50 cm). Using these reference measurements we can solve for the image locations of the ticks $\alpha_X=\alpha_Y=\alpha_Z=1$ m.

@fig-office_all_calibrated_box shows the final calibrated axes with ticks placed each 50 cm along each of the three axes.
concepts.motivation_md: Calibrating the projected world axis corrects for perspective distortion, enabling accurate placement of distance markers in images, which is essential for precise spatial measurements from single images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perspective projection distorts spacing of tick marks along axes in images.
- Use cross-ratio invariant to calibrate world coordinate projections.
- Reference object measurements enable solving for tick mark placements.

concepts.title: Locating a 3D Point
concepts.one_liner: We can estimate 3D coordinates of a point from a single image by using context such as the object's relation to the ground and vanishing points.
concepts.content:
In the absence of any other information, we cannot recover the 3D location of a single point $\mathbf{P}$ from a single view as illustrated in @fig-locating_a_3d_point [a]. But real world scenes are composed of a multitude of objects providing context, which allows solving the 3D estimation problem even with just a single image. In the previous section we showed how to estimate the height of an object; here we show how to estimate the 3D coordinates of a point.

The basic procedure is illustrated in @fig-locating_a_3d_point [b]. The trick consists in using context (what object is the point part of, where is the horizon line of the scene and where are the vanishing points) to estimate 3D from a single image. It suffices to know that the point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object that is in contact with the ground and the geometry of this object provides the information to localize the projection of the point $\mathbf{P}$ on the ground plane, which we denote with $\mathbf{G}$.

(see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...)

Once we know the image location of the projection of the 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ to the ground, $\mathbf{G}$, we can project this point to the world-coordinate axis. To estimate the $Y$-coordinate we use a similar method as the one described in the previous section. We first find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_3$, that passes by the point $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, and then find the intersection with the horizon line, giving the point $\mathbf{v}$. Next, find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_4$, that passes by $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. The intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ with the $Y_w$-axis gives the coordinate $P_y$. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates can be obtained by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ with the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.

- Use object's contact with ground and scene geometry to locate 3D points.
- Project point's ground projection and use vanishing points to find coordinates.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: We can extract camera parameters using only vanishing points under some conditions.
concepts.content:
In the previous chapters, we have seen different methods to calibrate a camera. We saw that we could do it by taking pictures of a calibration pattern, and we also showed that we can extract both the intrinsics and extrinsics from a set of 3D points and their image correspondences. Here we will see a different method that uses only the vanishing points to extract the camera parameters; note that this method will only work under some conditions.

The first step consists in finding the vanishing points in the image. Let's use the office picture from @fig-vanishing_lines. In this particular scene there are many parallel lines in 3D, and they also happen to be parallel to the three directions we used to define the world coordinates system. Therefore, the three vanishing points are also aligned with the world coordinate axis.

Let's assume that we have three orthogonal vanishing directions. That is the vectors $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ are orthogonal in 3D. From equation (@eq-vanishing_projection), the vanishing points measured on the image are the result of projecting $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ into the image using the unknown camera projection matrix. We will use the vanishing points to derive a set of constraints on the projection matrix. To do this, we start by inverting equation (@eq-vanishing_projection):
$$\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i
$$ {#eq-vanishing_projection_inv} Because the vectors $\mathbf{D}_i$ are orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Therefore, we can write:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j 
$$ {#eq-vanishing_projection_constraint} As $\mathbf{R}$ is an orthonormal matrix, we have that $\mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}$, resulting in a relationship that only depends on the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^T \mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0
$$

It is useful to define the following matrix:
$$\mathbf{W} =  \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$$ This is also known as the **conic matrix** and it has lots of different properties @Hartley2004. 

If we assume that the skew parameter of the intrinsic camera matrix is zero, then the matrix $\mathbf{W}$ has a very particular structure and it has only four different values: $$\mathbf{W} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & 0 & b\\
    0 & a & c\\
    b & c & d
    \end{bmatrix}$$ Using equation (@eq-vanishing_projection_constraint), we can derive a linear constraint on the values $a,b,c,d$ for each pair of vanishing points. Defining the vector $\mathbf{w}=[a~b~c~d]^\mathsf{T}$, we can rewrite equation (@eq-vanishing_projection_constraint) into a system of linear equations that has the form: $$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$$

The linear equation can be solved with the singular value decomposition (SVD) and the result is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue.

Once we have $\mathbf{W}$, we can find $\mathbf{K}$ by using the Cholesky factorization, which decomposes a matrix as the product of an upper triangular matrix and its transpose. The last step is to normalize the result by normalizing all the matrix values so that the value on the bottom-right side is 1. In our running example of the office picture, we get the following solution for $\mathbf{K}$: 

$$
\mathbf{K} = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    3{,}054.6    &      0    &     1{,}999.4\\
       0    &       3{,}054.6    &     1{,}528.3\\
       0    &          0    &          1
\end{bmatrix}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Using vanishing points for camera calibration allows extracting intrinsic parameters without special calibration patterns, useful when only images of scenes with orthogonal directions are available.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points correspond to directions of parallel lines in 3D.
- Orthogonal vanishing points impose constraints on camera intrinsics.
- Solve linear system from constraints to find intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$.

concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates allow us to represent points at infinity with finite coordinates by setting the last element to 0.
concepts.content:
Homogeneous coordinates offer an alternative way of working with vanishing points. Let's start by writing the parametric vector form of a 3D line using homogeneous coordinates:
$$\mathbf{P}_t = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    X_0 + t D_X\\
    Y_0 + t D_Y\\
    Z_0 + t D_Z\\
    1
    \end{bmatrix}
    =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    X_0/t + D_X\\
    Y_0 /t+ D_Y\\
    Z_0/t + D_Z\\
    1/t
    \end{bmatrix}
$$
The first term is equivalent to the writing of the line in equation (@eq-parametric_vector_line). As homogeneous coordinates are invariant to a global scaling, we can divide the vector by $t$ which results in the second equality. In the limit $t \to \infty$ the fourth coordinate of equation (@eq-parametric_vector_line_homogeneous) converges resulting in:
$$\mathbf{P}_\infty = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    D_X\\
    D_Y\\
    D_Z\\
    0
    \end{bmatrix}
    = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{D}\\
    0
    \end{bmatrix}$$
Note that here we are representing a point at infinity with finite homogeneous coordinates. This is another of the advantages of homogeneous coordinates. Homogeneous coordinates allow us to represent points at infinity with finite coordinates by setting the last element to 0.
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify working with points at infinity, such as vanishing points, by representing them with finite coordinate vectors where the last element is zero, enabling consistent mathematical treatment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Homogeneous coordinates represent 3D lines parametrically with an extra coordinate.
- Dividing by parameter $t$ leverages scale invariance to analyze behavior at infinity.
- Points at infinity have last homogeneous coordinate zero, allowing finite representation.

concepts.title: Horizon Line
concepts.one_liner: The horizon line is the line that passes by all the vanishing points of all the lines contained in a plane.
concepts.content:
Any 3D plane becomes a half-plane in the image and has a horizon line. The horizon line is the line that passes by all the vanishing points of all the lines contained in the plane as shown in @fig-palma_horizon.

(see figure: All parallel lines contained in a plane converge to a set of vanishing points. All those vanishing points are contained in the **horizon line** of the plane. Parallel planes have the same horizon...)

As parallel lines converge to the same vanishing point, parallel planes also have the same horizon line. In @fig-palma_horizon, the lines in the building facade that are parallel to the ground also converge to a vanishing point that lies on the horizon line. In this particular example, the lines in the facade also happen to be parallel to one of the axes of the floor tiles, converging to the same vanishing point on the right side of the figure.
concepts.motivation_md: The horizon line collects all vanishing points of lines in a plane, helping to understand the geometric structure and orientation of planes in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The horizon line passes through all vanishing points of lines in a plane.
- Parallel planes share the same horizon line.
- Vanishing points of lines parallel to the ground lie on the horizon line.

concepts.title: Detecting Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Vanishing points can be extracted automatically by detecting image edges and using RANSAC to group edges voting for vanishing points.
concepts.content:
@fig-vanishing_lines shows the office scene and three vanishing points computed manually. In this scene there are three dominant orientations along orthogonal directions. The three vanishing points are estimated by selecting pairs of long edges in the image corresponding to parallel 3D lines in the scene and finding their intersection.

(see figure: Most object boundaries in this photograph are oriented parallel to one of the world-coordinates reference frame (the world-coordinates frame is chosen in this way on purpose). All the parallel 3D...)

Vanishing points can be extracted automatically from images by first detecting image edges and their orientations (like we did in chapter @sec-simplesystem) and then using RANSAC (@sec-RANSAC) to group the edges: every pair of edges will vote for a vanishing point and the point with the largest support will be considered a vanishing point.

There are also learning-based approaches for vanishing point detection using graphical models @coughlan1999manhattan, or deep learning based approaches such as DeepVP @Chang2018DeepVPDL and NeurVPS @zhou2019neurvps.
concepts.motivation_md: Detecting vanishing points automatically enables understanding scene geometry and orientation from images, which is essential for many computer vision tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vanishing points can be found by intersecting pairs of edges corresponding to parallel 3D lines.
- Automatic detection uses edge orientation and RANSAC voting.
- Learning-based methods also exist, including graphical models and deep learning.

concepts.title: Cross-Ratio
concepts.one_liner: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is a projective invariant preserved under perspective projection.
concepts.content:
As we have discussed before, perspective projection transforms many aspects of the 3D world when projecting into the 2D image: angles between lines are not preserved, the relative lengths between lines is not preserved, parallel 3D lines do not project into 2D parallel lines in the image (unless they are also parallel to the camera plane), and so on. Fortunately, some geometric properties are preserved under perspective projection. For instance, straight lines remain straight. Are there other quantities that are preserved? The cross-ratio is one of those quantities.

The cross-ratio of four collinear points is defined by the expression:
$$CR \left( \mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4 \right) 
= 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right|}
{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right|}$$
where $\left| \mathbf{P}_i -\mathbf{P}_j \right|$ is the euclidean distance between points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and $\mathbf{P}_j$, using heterogeneous coordinates.

[FIGURE:c3a83d33f5a7a7b5 | A diagram showing four collinear points labeled $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, and $P_4$ arranged along a single pink line. The points are spaced out from bottom-left to top-right to illustrate the geometric...]

The cross-ratio is considered the most important projective invariant. Two sets of points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ related by a projective transformation, as shown in @fig-cross_ratio_description, have the same cross-ratio (regardless of the choice of origin $\mathbf{O}$ or scale factor). That is:
$$CR(\mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4) = CR(\mathbf{Q}_1,\mathbf{Q}_2,\mathbf{Q}_3,\mathbf{Q}_4)$$

(see figure: The set of points $\mathbf{P}$ are related to the points $\mathbf{Q}$ (and $\mathbf{R}$) by the cross-ratio. The point $\mathbf{R}_1$ is in infinity because the line connecting the points...)

The order in which these points are considered matters in the calculation. There are $4!=24$ possible orderings resulting in six different values. If two sets of points, related by a projection, have the same ordering, then their cross ratio will be preserved. We do not provide the proof for the cross-ratio invariant here.

When one of the points is at infinity, all the terms that contain that point are cancelled out (this can also be seen by taking a limit). In the case of the points $\mathbf{R}$ from @fig-cross_ratio_description we get that cross-ratio is:
$$CR(\mathbf{R}_1,\mathbf{R}_2,\mathbf{R}_3,\mathbf{R}_4) = 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{R}_4 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right| }
{ \left| \mathbf{R}_3 - \mathbf{R}_2 \right|}$$
This value is equal to the cross-ratio of the points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.

To gain some intuition about the cross-ratio invariant, let's look at an empirical demonstration. @fig-cross_ratio_rulers shows a ruler seen under different view points. The blue dots correspond to same ruler locations with $P_1=0$ in, $P_2=6$ in, $P_3=8$ in, and $P_4=10$ in (we are making these measurements in inches, but note that the units do not affect the cross-ratio as it is scale invariant). Using those measurements, the cross-ratio is: $(8 \times 4)/(2 \times 10) = 1.6$. The same cross-ratio is obtained if we measure the positions of the four points using image coordinates and measuring distances in the image plane.

(see figure: Empirical demonstration of the cross-ratio invariant. You can check that measuring distances between the three dots on each image and computing the cross-ratio results in the value 1.6 for the three...)
concepts.motivation_md: The cross-ratio exists because it is a geometric quantity preserved under perspective projection, allowing consistent measurements despite distortions like foreshortening and angle changes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cross-ratio is defined for four collinear points and is preserved under projective transformations.
- It remains invariant even when one point is at infinity.
- Cross-ratio helps relate distances in 3D and their projections in images.

concepts.title: Measuring the Height of an Object
concepts.one_liner: We use the cross-ratio invariant and geometric constructions to estimate the height of an object from a reference object's height in an image.
concepts.content:
The problem we will address in this section is how to measure the height of one object given the height of a reference object in the scene. As shown in @fig-office_measuring_desk_setup, the height of the bookshelf is $h_{\text{bookshelf}}=197$ cm (in this example we will make our measurements using centimeters, but again, the choice of units is not important as long as all the measurements are consistent). Can we use this information together with the geometry of the scene to estimate the height of the desk, $h_{\text{desk}}$?

(see figure: Given the height of a reference object, the location of the horizon line and one vanishing point, how can we estimate the height of other objects in the scene?)

Due to perspective projection, we can not directly compare the relative height of the desk with respect to the height of the bookshelf using distances measured over the image. In order to be able to compare 3D distances using 2D image distances both objects need to be put in correspondence first. The bookshelf height is the distance between the 3D points that correspond to the 2D locations of the bottom of the bookshelf, $\mathbf{g}_b$, and the top of the bookshelf, $\mathbf{t}_b$. Similarly, the desk height is the distance between the 3D points that correspond to $\mathbf{g}_d$ and $\mathbf{t}_d$. We can not use directly the points $\mathbf{g}_b$ and $\mathbf{t}_b$, and $\mathbf{g}_d$ and $\mathbf{t}_d$ as they are given in image coordinates. In order to be able to use distances in the image domain we need to first translate the points defining the desk height on top of the bookshelf, and then use the cross-ratio invariant to relate the ratio between image distances with the ratios of 3D heights.

In the rest, all the vectors refer to image coordinates in homogeneous coordinates. Let's start by projecting the desk height onto the bookshelf. To do this we need to follow several steps:

-   Estimate the line that passes by the ground points $\mathbf{g}_d$ and $\mathbf{g}_b$. Using homogeneous coordinates, the line can be computed using the cross-product:
    $$\boldsymbol{l}_1 = \mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b$$

-   Compute the intersection of the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ as:
    $$\mathbf{a} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \mathbf{h}$$ As the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ is on the ground plane, the point $\mathbf{a}$ is the vanishing point of line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$.

-   Compute the line that passes by $\mathbf{a}$ and the top of the desk $\mathbf{t}_d$ as:
    $$\boldsymbol{l}_2 = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{t}_d$$ Lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ are parallel on 3D and vertically aligned.

-   Finally we can compute where line $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ intersects with the bookshelf in the image plane which in this case will also correspond to an intersection of the corresponding 3D lines. We first compute the line that connects the bottom and top points of the bookshelf $\boldsymbol{l}_3 = \mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b$, and now we obtain the intersection with $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ as:
    $$\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{l}_2 \times \boldsymbol{l}_3$$

We can write all the previous steps into a single equation:
$$\mathbf{b} = (((\mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_d) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
Point $\mathbf{b}$ is the location where the top of the desk will be if we physically rearrange the furniture to bring the desk and the bookshelf into contact. The segment between points $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{g}_b$ is the projection of the desk height on the bookshelf. However, due to the foreshortening effect induced by perspective projection, we cannot simply rely on the ratio of image distances to estimate the desk's true height. Instead, we will utilize the cross-ratio invariant to make this estimation.

As J. J. Gibson pointed out, the ground plane is very useful for all kinds of 3D scene measurements.

In order to use the cross-ratio invariant we need two sets of four colinear points related by a projective geometry. @fig-office_measuring_desk_sketch shows a sketch of the setup we have in @fig-office_measuring_desk.

![Projection of desk height onto the bookshelf. We start with the bottom and top image coordinates of points along vertical edges of the bookshelf: 
$\mathbf{t}_b = [702~~2{,}958]^\mathsf{T}$ 
$\mathbf{g}_b= [987~~618]^\mathsf{T}$ 
and the desk: 
$\mathbf{t}_d = [679~~1{,}018]^\mathsf{T}$ 
$\mathbf{g}_d= [793~~59]^\mathsf{T}$ 
We compute the points 
$\mathbf{a}= [4{,}471~~2{,}486]^\mathsf{T}$ 
and
$\mathbf{b}= [2{,}237~~2{,}765]^\mathsf{T}$ 
as described in the text.](figures/single_view_3d/office_measuring_desk.png){width="85%" #fig-office_measuring_desk}

In the image plane, we have the four image points $\mathbf{t}_b$, $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{g}_b$ and $\mathbf{v}_3$. Those four 2D image points correspond to the 3D locations given by the top of the bookshelf, desk height, ground and infinity (which is the location of the vertical vanishing point in 3D).

(see figure: Sketch of the setting from @fig-office_measuring_desk. There are two sets of colinear points related by central projection. Their cross-ratios are identical.)

The rest of calculations requires computing distances between points, which only works when using heterogeneous coordinates (or homogeneous coordinates if the last component is equal to 1 for all points). The cross-ratio invariant between both sets of four points gives as the equality:

$$CR(\mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4) = CR(\mathbf{p}_1,\mathbf{p}_2,\mathbf{p}_3,\mathbf{p}_4)
$$
The left side of the equality corresponds to the distances between the 3D points and the right side to the distances of the image points measured in pixel units. As $\mathbf{P}_1$ is in infinity (as it corresponds to the vanishing point), the left side ratio only has two terms, resulting in the ratio between the bookshelf and desk heights. To compute the hand side we need the coordinates of the corresponding four image points. Those are provided in @fig-office_measuring_desk. Replacing all those values in equation (@eq-cross_ratio_shelf_desk) we obtain: 

$$\frac{h_{\text{bookshelf}}}{h_{\text{desk}}} = 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{v}_3 \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{g}_b \right| }{\left| \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{g}_b \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{v}_3  \right|}$$

The only unknown value in this equality is the height of the desk, $h_{\text{desk}}$, which results in $h_{\text{desk}} \simeq 73.1$ cm, which is close to the actual height of the desk (which is around 76 cm).

- Use cross-ratio invariant to relate image distances to actual heights.
- Project desk height onto bookshelf using line intersections and horizon line.
- Calculate desk height from known bookshelf height and image measurements.

concepts.title: Height Propagation to Supported Objects
concepts.one_liner: Height of objects not on the ground can be estimated by propagating height information through supporting objects using cross-ratio invariants.
concepts.content:
The method described in the previous section relies on using vertical lines in contact with the ground plane to propagate information from one point in space to another in order to make measurements. The method can not work if we can not establish the vertical projection of a point into the ground plane (or any other plane of reference). But once we have estimated the height of objects that are in contact with the ground, we can use them to propagate 3D information to other objects not directly on top of the ground. We can estimate the height of objects that are not in contact with the ground if they are on top of objects of known height. As an example, let's estimate the red bottle's height, which we can do after we estimated the height of the desk.

@fig-office_measuring_bottle shows how to estimate the height of the bottle.

(see figure: Estimating the height of the red bottle. For an object not in the ground we can propagate information from the objects that support it.)

As before, we will project the bottle height on the reference line on the corner of the bookshelf. To do this we need to find two vertically aligned parallel 3D lines that connect the bottle's top and bottom points with the bookshelf. The first line, $\boldsymbol{l}_1$, is the line connecting the bottom of the bottle, $\mathbf{g}_e$, and the point $\mathbf{b}$. These two points are at the same height from the ground plane as $\mathbf{b}$ corresponds to the top of the desk and $\mathbf{g}_e$ is the point of the bottle that is in contact with the top of the desk. The intersection of the line $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ give us point $\mathbf{a}$. Connecting point $\mathbf{a}$ with the top of the bottle, point $\mathbf{t}_e$, gives us the second line, $\boldsymbol{l}_2$. The intersection of this line with the reference bookshelf line is the point $\mathbf{c}$. The distance between the point $\mathbf{c}$ and the ground in 3D is the sum $h_{\text{bookshelf}}+h_{\text{desk}}$. Writing everything into a compact equation results in:
$$\mathbf{c} = (((\mathbf{g}_e \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_e) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
Note that this equation relies on having computed $\mathbf{b}$ first.

Using the cross-ratio invariant we arrive to the following equation:
$$h_{\text{bottle}} =
h_{\text{bookshelf}}  \frac{\left| \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{g}_b \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{v}_3  \right|}{\left| \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{v}_3 \right| \left| \mathbf{t}_b - \mathbf{g}_b \right| }  - h_{\text{desk}}$$
This last equation shows how the height of the bottle is estimated by propagating information from the ground via its supporting object, the desk. Learning based approaches that estimated 3D from single images will have to perform such propagation implicitly. The result that we get is $h_{\text{bottle}} \simeq 27.6$ cm which is close to the real height of 25.5 cm.

concepts.one_liner: The Ames room is a distorted room that creates a powerful 3D visual illusion, appearing rectangular from a specific viewpoint despite its irregular shape.
concepts.content:
3D visual illusions are remarkably powerful. One captivating 3D illusion is the Ames room.

The Ames room is an irregularly shaped room constructed so that when viewed with one eye from a particular vantage point, it appears perfectly rectangular. This effect is achieved by making the part of the wall farther from the viewer larger so it appears fronto-parallel.

Geometric description of the Ames room visual illusion.

[FIGURE:4b865b0ab7d9d5dd | A floor plan diagram of an Ames room illusion showing an irregular trapezoidal 'Actual room floor plan' and a dashed rectangular 'Perceived room floor plan'. Two red lines originate from a 'Pinhole'...]

The best way to understand this illusion is by building and experiencing it yourself. Instructions are in @fig-ames_room. Looking through the aperture on the front wall indicated by "cut," the room appears square and smaller than it actually is, seeming as if viewed from the middle despite the opening being closer to the right wall.

(see figure: Make your own Ames room. Take a picture of this page and print it as large as you can (A4 or letter size will be sufficient). When you look through the aperture on the *front wall*, the room will...)

This illusion is especially remarkable when the room is large enough for people to walk in. As people walk along the back wall, they appear to change height, defying strong prior expectations about their appearance. @fig-ames_room_cat illustrates this with a cut-out version of the Ames room.

[FIGURE:db734c72cbd8a0cd | A photograph of a physical model of an Ames room constructed from paper. A LEGO minifigure stands on the left side of the room, appearing much larger than the surrounding architecture due to the...]

[FIGURE:845b1e8c4509a400 | A photograph of a physical model of an Ames room, which is a distorted room that creates an optical illusion of depth. A LEGO minifigure stands in the right corner, appearing much larger than the...]

If an object is placed along the back wall of the Ames room shown in @fig-ames_room, its perceived size changes. Also, both doors appear similar in size despite being quite different in reality.

concepts.title: Projection of 3D Lines
concepts.one_liner: In perspective projection, 3D lines project into 2D lines in the camera plane, parameterized by a point and a direction vector.
concepts.content:
In perspective projection, 3D lines project into 2D lines in the camera plane. We can write the parametric vector form of a 3D line using heterogeneous coordinates. A 3D line can be parameterized by a point $\mathbf{P}_0 = [X_0, Y_0, Z_0]^\mathsf{T}$ and a direction vector $\mathbf{D} = [D_X, D_Y, D_Z]^\mathsf{T}$ as:

$$\mathbf{P}_t = \begin{bmatrix} X_0 + t D_x\\ Y_0 + t D_y\\ Z_0 + t D_z \end{bmatrix}$$

The point $\mathbf{P}_t$ moves along the line as the parameter $t$ varies from $-\infty$ to $\infty$. A camera located at the world coordinate origin observes a 2D line resulting from projecting this 3D line onto the camera plane, as illustrated in @fig-vanishing_points.

concepts.title: Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Vanishing points are finite points in the image where projections of parallel 3D lines converge under perspective projection.
concepts.content:
Even though a line in 3D space extends infinitely, its 2D projection does not. According to equation (@eq-line_projection), as the parameter $t$ approaches infinity, the projected line converges to a finite point called the vanishing point:

$$\mathbf{v} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbf{p}_t = \left [ \begin{array}{c} f \dfrac{D_X}{D_Z}\\[12pt] f \dfrac{D_Y}{D_Z} \end{array} \right ]$$

The vanishing point $\mathbf{v} = [v_x, v_y]^\mathsf{T}$ depends only on the direction vector $\mathbf{D}$. Thus, all parallel 3D lines project into 2D lines that converge to the same vanishing point in the image. If $D_Z = 0$, the 3D line is parallel to the camera plane and the vanishing point is at infinity.

@fig-vanishing_lines_and_planes shows sets of parallel 3D lines and their 2D projections. Each group of parallel lines converges to a distinct vanishing point. Lines parallel to the camera plane remain parallel and converge to a vanishing point at infinity.
